extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of comic/satirical character sketches (general Victorian-humor audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and/or compose comic character portraits of various 'young gentleman' archetypes (censorious, funny, theatrical, poetical, boastful, and ladies'-favorite) using behavioral detail, dialogue, and social-reaction cues. Useful for satire, characterization, or humorous social observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorious Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: A criticising young man who pronounces sharp judgments on music, pictures, books, poetry, and people at a glance; professes not to be severe yet always finds fault and speaks in a way that influences others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key markers: repeats words when at a loss; smiles contemptuously while making pronouncements; delivers decisive but shallow observations (e.g., 'Did you observe her manner? — that’s all I ask.'); his nods and pursed lips prompt others to accept his judgments. Use small gestures and formulaic phrases to signal his censoriousness. Example: turning a casual remark into a whispered 'Mr. Fairfax has observed something exceedingly odd in Mrs. Barker’s manner.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The Funny Young Gentleman (Mr. Griggins archetype)
rubrics_metrics.description: A boisterous, clownish social entertainer who attracts loud laughter by outrageous, often physical, comic antics and topical puns; acts with high spirits and behaves with irreverent familiarity toward people and things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features and examples: dramatic entrance (startling knock); pantomime-like contortions; comic imitations of stage-clowns; puns and silly conceits ('love among the roses'); intrusive physical jokes (sitting in laps, snuffing a candle which sets someone's hair on fire); stealing food/drink, masking to frighten children, producing mistletoe for general kissing. Note social dynamics: despite scandalised protestations, such a fellow often remains popular, especially with women and children. Use exaggerated action, impudence, and irrepressible good-humour to create this type.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Theatrical Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: A theatre-obsessed young man who speaks as an insider about plays and actors, uses pet nicknames for theatres and performers, reveres stage conventions, and judges drama by spectacle and conventional stage business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits: breathless reporting of backstage news; shorthand names for venues (Covent-Garden = 'the garden'); celebrity gossip (marriages, name-changes); reverence for stagecraft (trap-doors, huge crowded final scenes); preference for extravagance and violent, redundant action onstage; formulaic reading of 'natural' expressions (specific frowns, winks, stamps). Use precise theatrical jargon, confident-but-shallow anecdotes, and a tendency to accept bills/playbills at face value. He defends established theatrical conventions against criticism ('it always has been done in that way').

rubrics_metrics.name: The Poetical Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentimental or pseudo-poetic young man with plaintive mien and affectations: abstracted, unkempt, given to grandiose melancholy, hyperbolic language, and imitation of gloomy poetic tropes without deep substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markers: lounging with eyes fixed on the ceiling, sudden pencil-scribbles of a few words, dramatic sighs and slaps on the head, wearing uncut hair, melodramatic admiration for grim events and even criminals, grandiose superlatives ('grandest, greatest, noblest'), and composing stanzas addressed to Bank of England, St. Paul's, or a violet. He quotes gloomy authors and frames himself as an 'outcast' or 'great spirit.' To portray him: emphasize affectation, overblown diction, and inconsistent talent (occasional contributions to 'Lady’s Magazine' or album verses).

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'Throwing-off' (Bragging) Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: A boastful impostor who loudly 'throws off' tales of inherited wealth, extraordinary accomplishments, high-born relatives, and wide acquaintanceship—usually fraudulent or exaggerated and aimed at impressing (especially young women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: boasts of a wealthy Irish father/ancestors with magnificent castles and libraries; claims unrivalled skill in every sport but 'out of practice'; slips in intimations of past engagements to excite sympathy; name-drops distant or convenient acquaintances to win disputes; blends compliments to a lady with self-aggrandising remarks. Examples include false military affectations (cap with gold band) and fake musical ability. Social warning included: 'Ladies, ladies, the throwing-off young gentlemen are often swindlers, and always fools.' Use confident, digressive bragging and implausible specifics to signal this type.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Young Ladies’ Young Gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: The young man adored by young ladies: handsome (fresh color, white teeth, whiskers), constantly smiling, flattering, and attentive—adept at small gallantries, flirting, and charmingly monopolising female attention during social outings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical behaviors: punctual/unpunctual charm (arrival forgiven), flirtatious banter and modest boasts (dancing with an heiress), playful physical skirmishes (capture of a rosebud), winning gifts by winks or tricks (wins gloves from sleeping ladies), eating from ladies' plates and being served attentively, and conducting light, diverting conversation on outings. Use polished manners, casual flirtation, and theatrical but genial self-possession to create him (example: Mr. Balim at the Epping Forest party).
